messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Politician
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Viktor Novak

Viktor Novak was sixty-eight years old and had spent forty-two years in state politics—first as a city councillor, then as a state representative, and for the last decade and a half as a senator. He had built a reputation for steady pragmatism, for showing up to ribbon cuttings and constituent meetings with the same measured presence he brought to budget negotiations. His wife, Patricia, had learned long ago that his steadiness was both his gift and his armor. What she did not know, until the past eight months, was that the armor had fractured.

The accident had occurred on a Tuesday evening in March, on Route 9 heading north toward the capitol. Viktor had been alone, driving home after a late committee session, thinking through the language of a healthcare bill. A pickup truck crossed the center line without warning—the driver later tested positive for alcohol—and struck the passenger side of his sedan at sixty miles per hour. The impact came as a series of frozen moments: the sudden lurch of the steering wheel, the shriek of metal, the sensation of the car rolling, the ceiling becoming the wall becoming the floor. He remembered the smell—sharp, acrid, chemical—and then nothing until the paramedics were cutting him out of the wreckage. Two broken ribs, a fractured collarbone, lacerations across his left side. He had been lucky, everyone said. He had walked away.

But Viktor had not walked away. He had remained in that moment, fragmented into snapshots that returned without warning. The image of the truck's grille filling his window. The sight of his own blood on the airbag. These moments came back as discrete pictures, vivid and unconnected, and when he tried to describe them to Patricia or to the emergency room physician, the narrative would dissolve. He would begin to explain and then lose the thread entirely, the words scattering like the glass that had covered the road.

What troubled him most was what he had come to believe about himself. The accident, in his mind, was not random. It was not the result of another man's recklessness or impairment. Viktor had come to see it as something he had brought upon himself—a consequence of the sort of man he was. He had been distracted that evening, thinking about the bill rather than the road. He had taken Route 9 instead of the interstate; if he had chosen differently, he would have been miles away when the truck crossed the line. These thoughts circled endlessly. He dwelt on the decisions that had led him to that exact moment, and each time he arrived at the same conclusion: he had done this to himself. The rumination was relentless. Even in the quiet moments before sleep, he would find himself retracing his choices, assigning blame, turning the accident over in his mind like a stone he could not put down.

The physical pain had faded by June, but something else had taken its place. When the memories returned—and they returned often, especially in the evenings—he felt the pain again, sharp and localized, in his ribs and across his left shoulder, as though his body was remembering what his mind could not fully articulate. More disturbing still was the sense that he was marked. When he returned to the capitol in May, he was certain that people could see what had happened to him simply by looking at his face. He imagined they could read the accident in his expression, that his weakness was visible, that he had been exposed in some fundamental way.

By late August, Viktor had stopped driving. He had also stopped being a passenger, which meant he had begun declining invitations to events outside walking distance of his home. He asked Patricia to drive him to necessary appointments, and even then, he found himself tense, watching the road obsessively, certain that another collision was imminent. The silence of the car—the absence of conversation or music—made him feel as though something catastrophic was about to happen. He had to be on guard constantly. At night, he woke at irregular intervals, seized by the need to verify that he was safe, that the house was secure, that Patricia was still there beside him. His concentration, once his professional hallmark, had become unreliable. During a committee meeting in July, he had lost his place mid-sentence, unable to recover the thread of his own argument.

Patricia had finally insisted that he see someone. She had watched him withdraw from colleagues, decline speaking engagements, and spend increasing hours alone in his study. She had heard him, in the dark, blaming himself for decisions made months before the accident. When she suggested that what had happened to him—the trauma itself, not his choices—might require professional help, Viktor had resisted. But the weight of it had become unbearable. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally flawed, that the accident had revealed something true about his character. He was terrified that if he stopped vigilant, if he let his guard down, something worse would happen. And he was desperate to understand why he could not simply move forward, why a man who had spent four decades managing crises and maintaining composure had become undone by a single moment he could not control.
